Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Vignette:
At sixty-seven, Marcus Tuala had spent forty years transforming other people’s homes into sanctuaries—spaces of light, proportion, and calm. He was known for his patience, his meticulous eye, and the way he could make a room breathe. Now, he could barely step into his own office. The trauma that had undone him had happened three years earlier, during a business trip to the Middle East, when he was taken captive by armed men during a hotel siege. For eleven hours, he was held in a windowless storage room with seven other hostages, blindfolded, his hands bound. The men shouted at them in Arabic—commands, threats, he never knew which—and he had been certain he was going to die. He had been certain, too, that he would never see his wife again. She had died two years before that, and he had sometimes wondered if the terror of the captivity had been sharpened by the knowledge that there was no one waiting for him on the other side.

Since returning home, Marcus had found that the world had become a series of traps. The trigger could be almost anything: a raised voice in a restaurant, a door that clicked shut too firmly, the sound of a language he did not understand. But the worst was the shouting. He would be walking down the street in Honolulu and hear a man call out in Arabic on his phone, and suddenly Marcus would be back in that storage room, his heart slamming against his ribs, his palms slick, his mind gone blank. His body reacted before he had even registered what he had heard—a lurch, a freeze, a desperate scan for an exit. He had come to believe that he was no longer safe anywhere. He could not bear to have his back to an open space. In restaurants, he insisted on a booth against the wall, and even then he found himself turning his head constantly, checking the door, checking the faces. He had begun to rehearse conversations before any interaction—calling a client, ordering coffee, greeting a neighbor—running through possible lines in his head because he was terrified that if he was caught off guard, he would lose his words, and then he would look weak, and then something bad would happen.

The avoidance had crept in slowly, then swallowed him whole. He stopped going to his design studio altogether. At first, he told himself it was just a break—too many memories of the trip, too much noise. But weeks became months, and he found he could not bring himself to walk through the door. The building had a small elevator, and the thought of stepping into that enclosed box, the doors sliding shut, the air growing still—it was impossible. He began working from home, taking only clients who agreed to meet at his kitchen table. His business shrank. His income dropped. He told himself it was temporary, but he knew, in the hollow hours of the night, that he was hiding.

The memories themselves had become strange. Sometimes he could recall the event in perfect detail—the smell of sweat and dust, the pressure of the zip-ties—but he felt nothing. It was as if it had happened to someone else, a man he watched from a great distance, numb and untroubled. And then, without warning, the sound would come back: a shout, a curse, a phrase he did not understand but could still hear as clearly as the day it was screamed. When he tried to tell his sister what had happened, he would lose the thread halfway through, stumbling over words, unable to finish the sentence, and he would stop trying.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was not the fear, but the loneliness. He had been widowed for five years, and for the first time, he felt entirely cut off from the world. He could not work. He could not visit friends. He could not sit in a room without checking the walls. He came to a therapist because he was afraid that if he did not, he would spend the rest of his life in his kitchen, back to the wall, rehearsing the same conversations with no one.
